_comment: Vocabularies @arthome/core keeps to itself: every member appears in NEITHER
contract, deliberately. `check-vocabulary.py` reads this file and RETRACTS an
entry the day one of its members reaches a wire — a stale exemption is an
error here, not a silent pass.
Keyed by NAME rather than by location, and that distinction is the rule: put an
exemption in the artefact when the only stable key would be a LOCATION (a
contract block has no name, so its `source: none` lives inline), and in a side
file when there is a stable NAME. A vocabulary has one.
It is a side file for a second reason: the claim is about the PAIR, not about
the domain. @arthome/core should not carry assertions about what the wire does.
Being domain-only is a claim that nothing serves these values. It is not a
place to park a vocabulary that has not been published yet — that one is a
finding, and it should stay red until it is published or genuinely internal.
EMPTY, AND THAT IS THE POINT. `MESSAGE_DOMAINS` was exempted here on 2026-09-24
and the exemption has been WITHDRAWN: the project lead ruled it a contract defect,
not a domain-only vocabulary. The i18n theme survives only inside an artifact URL,
and `a value recoverable only by parsing a string is a value the contract did not
serve` — `LabelCatalogRef` already carries `domain`, so publishing it restores a
field rather than inventing one.
The lesson for whoever adds the next entry: being hard to express on the wire is
not the same as being internal. The test is whether anything OUTSIDE the domain
needs the value — not whether a way to send it already exists.

allow.reason: Internal guards, not refusals. Every member fires on a value that never came from a client: summing two currencies, a malformed instant INSIDE the system, a rate outside 0-10000. A malformed value arriving from a surface is refused at the boundary as `api.schema_invalid`, before any rule runs, so no contract can produce these and no surface has anything to render for one. Publishing them would be a contract promising errors it cannot emit. The split was made when check-vocabulary's inverse check reported 23 domain codes reaching neither contract - a true finding with two causes mixed together, and this is the half that is correct rather than pending.

Reaches the documents through `x-arthome-upstream`, not through `x-arthome-vocabulary`, so this gate cannot see it — it reads member lists on fields, and an upstream is an annotation on an OPERATION. R22 in check-openapi.py compares every one of them against UPSTREAMS, which spreads this list. Declared here so the inverse check states what it cannot reach rather than reporting a gap that another gate covers.

Same position as SERVICES, which it spreads. It adds `realtime`, which is NOT a service: two operations read the real-time gateway's Redis resume buffer, and their own comments say so — the annotation was right about the dependency and wrong about the category, so anyone counting upstreams got eight services out of seven. R22 is what compares it.

The payment provider's own status for an intent (adr-payments.md §4), read by the domain to decide an order's transition and never relayed as itself: a surface reads `Order.state` and, while awaiting payment, `PaymentHandoff.state`, both `ORDER_STATES`. Nothing outside the domain asks a provider's intent whether it is `requires_action` or `succeeded` — that is exactly the translation `settleConfirmedPayment` performs.

What a provider's webhook says happened to an intent, a refund or a dispute, recorded on `stripe_event_inbox` before anything reads it (adr-payments.md §7.2) and consumed by the worker that applies it: `refund_succeeded` settles a refund, moving a cancelled seat to `refunded`, and `dispute_opened` moves the order to `disputed`. It is a fact the domain reacts to, never a value any surface polls or displays: a surface reads `Order.state` and `TicketCard.state`.

A `SeatHold`'s own bookkeeping (data-model.md §3.2): whether the capacity behind a purchase is still claimed, spent, timed out or given back. A surface never asks for a hold; it reads `Order.state` and `TicketCard.state`, which the hold's transitions cause but do not mirror one for one — `consumed` and `released` both resolve to an order that has already moved on.

The account's lifecycle as identity records it (data-model.md §1.1), read by identity to decide whether a credential may open a session. A surface reads the consequences, never the status: a refused sign-in, and the account deletion screen's own `DeletionState`, which describes the request rather than the account.

The `iss` of the token a BFF mints for each call to a service (adr-auth.md §8). It travels from a BFF to a service and nowhere else: no client ever obtains a service-audience token (§8.2.1 does not relay `/token`), so neither contract can carry one.

Which intent a `SeatHold`'s expiry belongs to — a direct checkout or a TV pairing (data-model.md §3.2) — kept to size the hold's duration (`HOLD_MINUTES_CHECKOUT` versus `HOLD_MINUTES_TV_PAIRING`). Internal sizing, never served: neither purchase path tells a surface which one it took.
